analysis.one_liner: Requires federally funded drug inventions to have reasonable pricing agreements before patents are granted.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors, was never taken up by its committee, and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: When federal money pays for health research that produces a new drug, biologic, or medical technology, the bill would require whoever receives the patent to sign a 'reasonable pricing' agreement with the Department of Health and Human Services before getting the patent. The government could not be charged more for the drug than the lowest price charged in comparable wealthy countries. The Secretary could waive the requirement only after public notice and comment.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and patients. Drugs developed with public research dollars would have to be priced reasonably as a condition of receiving the patent, and the federal government (including Medicare and Medicaid, the biggest buyers) would pay no more than the lowest price charged in major wealthy OECD countries [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, taxpayers, and federal health programs

how_it_helps.text: Bars federal agencies and nonprofits from transferring a patent on a drug, biologic, or other health technology developed with federal funding until the recipient signs a reasonable pricing agreement with HHS [S2][S3].

Requires that the federal government be charged no more than the lowest price charged for the same drug in OECD countries with large economies and at least half of U.S. per-capita income, effectively benchmarking U.S. prices to what other developed countries pay [S3].
Prohibits pricing formulas or contract terms that give foreign buyers better access or terms than U.S. buyers, including limits on supply [S3].
Any waiver of the pricing requirement requires public notice, an opportunity to comment, and a written public-interest finding, so decisions to skip reasonable pricing happen in the open [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical companies and other patent recipients licensing federally funded inventions would earn less on those drugs than under current law, and universities and nonprofits that profit from licensing publicly funded research would see a cap on that revenue [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill never defines what makes a price 'reasonable,' leaving the standard to HHS's discretion and making outcomes depend heavily on how a given administration interprets it [S3].

Companies might decline to license inventions from federally funded research rather than accept pricing conditions, which could delay turning public laboratory discoveries into actual medicines — an objection HHS itself raised when it removed a similar 'reasonable pricing' clause in 1999, saying it may have driven firms away from licensing NIH inventions.
The bill reaches only drugs and technologies whose patents trace to federally funded research, so it would not touch the pricing of the majority of drugs developed with private money [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — that taxpayers should not pay premium prices for drugs invented with their own money, and should not pay more than peer countries — is straightforward and popular. The main honest costs are that a vague 'reasonable pricing' standard invites inconsistent enforcement, and that conditions on patents could make some companies walk away from licensing public research, potentially slowing commercialization. Its scope is also narrow: it covers only federally funded inventions, not drug prices generally. Even so, it died without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, so none of these tradeoffs were ever debated on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate health committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on July 31, 2017 [S1][S5].
It was read twice and referred the same day to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No cosponsors signed on at any point [S4].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — ever occurred, and the bill died at the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical companies and research institutions that license federally funded inventions keep the current system, in which patents on public research are transferred with no pricing conditions. Patients and federal programs gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill; the only member of the Senate to attach his name to it.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Sen. Lamar Alexander, R-TN)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the entire 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no senator besides Sanders signed on — no Republican and no Democrat — so no party lineup ever formed; the bill simply sat in committee untouched [S4][S5].

industries.note: Companies licensing drugs invented with federal research money would have to accept 'reasonable pricing' conditions and would be barred from charging the U.S. government more than the lowest price in peer countries, cutting revenue on those products. Under current law they receive such patents unconditionally.

Universities and nonprofits that hold patents on federally funded inventions profit from licensing them to drug makers; the bill would cap that revenue by conditioning every transfer on a pricing agreement. Some firms might decline to license rather than accept the terms, reducing the institutions' income but keeping the technology publicly priced.

As the largest buyers of prescription drugs, federal programs would pay no more than the lowest price charged in major OECD countries for federally developed drugs, lowering taxpayer and beneficiary costs.
